problem: Existing human-aware navigation simulators mostly use crowd-movement models in which every agent behaves identically, and they lack varied individual reactions to the robot. They are also tied to ROS 1 or Unity, and each ships its own closed, incompatible metric set.
motivation: Real experiments with people are costly, hard to replicate and risky, so realistic simulated humans are needed. Social navigation evaluation must cover safety and comfort as well as efficiency, yet there is no agreed metric set. Computing metrics without modelling the different ways people react to a robot can give wrong or unclear results.
key_idea: An open-source ROS 2 human navigation simulator that extends the Social Force Model with behavior-tree-driven individual reactions to the robot (regular, impassive, surprised, curious, scared, threatening) and bundles a configurable evaluator with 28 social-navigation metrics, plus a Gazebo wrapper.
insight: Per-behavior metric breakdowns expose differences that aggregate metrics hide. In the Combined scenario, threatening agents produce far more intimate-space intrusion (about 45-58%) than regular agents (0%) for all planners. The 3-planner comparison shows that planners with distance-only social costs (SCL) do well on distance metrics, while a planner using social work (SFW) does best on force-based metrics. A broad metric set is therefore needed to characterize planners.
method: Architecture: a hunav manager module receives agent states from a simulator wrapper via ROS 2 service calls, computes each agent's next state, and returns it; agents are configured via a YAML file or an RViz panel.
Human navigation model: Social Force Model with its group extension drives the agents, and the robot is treated as either a pedestrian or an obstacle depending on the behavior.

Behavior set: regular, impassive (robot as an obstacle), surprised (stops and looks at the robot), curious (approaches slowly, loses interest after 30 s), scared (extra repulsive force and lower max speed), threatening (blocks the robot's path, gives up after 40 s).
Behavior trees: BehaviorTree.CPP structures the switching between tasks, so behaviors are easy to modify or add.

Gazebo wrapper: a world generator writes agents and a plugin into the world file, and the plugin updates actor poses each step by talking to HuNavSim; it ships with cafeteria, warehouse and house scenarios and new 3D human models with animations.

HuNavEvaluator: records the experiment and computes 28 selectable metrics (from Pérez et al., SEAN 2.0, SocNavBench, Katyal et al. and SFM-based work); it writes general, per-time-step, per-behavior-group and per-behavior time-step files.

setting.backbone: Social Force Model + behavior trees (rule-based simulator); evaluated planners are ROS 2 Nav2 DWB, DWB + Social Costmap Layer, and a Social Force Window (SFW) planner
setting.observation: simulator state of the robot and human agents (poses and velocities); the planners use Nav2 local costmaps
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands for a mobile robot
setting.simulator: Gazebo (via the HuNavSim wrapper; Morse and Webots are named as possible bases)
setting.privileged: Agent poses and velocities from the simulator are used for the metrics and by the social planners.

numbers_note: The paper is a simulator/benchmarking tool paper for social navigation and has no results on the canonical embodied-navigation benchmarks. Its tables (II-IV) compare three planners (DWB, SCL, SFW) on custom Passing, Crossing and Combined scenarios; these are baselines, not the paper's own method, so they are not listed.
results: The tool produces 28 metrics that differentiate the DWB, SCL and SFW planners. In the Crossing scenario SFW has the lowest social work (0.88, vs 1.33 for DWB and 2.20 for SCL) and the lowest intimate-space intrusion (1.6%, vs 13.7% and 14.6%). In the Combined scenario, threatening agents cause 45-58% intimate-space intrusion for all planners, versus 0% for regular agents.
limitations: The validation is small: 10 runs per planner in simple scenarios (Passing, Crossing, Combined) with only three planners, and no comparison to real human data or a realism validation of the behaviors.
Only the Social Force Model and a few scripted behaviors are supported, only a Gazebo wrapper exists, and body animation realism is out of scope.
The metric compilation is incomplete (28 metrics), with CrowdBot and other metrics still to be added.
